title: Piles (Arsha): Ayurvedic Causes, Diet & Daily Care
excerpt: Bleeding during stools, burning, itching, pain or a wart-like swelling at the anus — piles are a very common problem, but out of embarrassment people often keep hiding it. Learn the causes from the Ayurvedic view, the difference between piles, fissure and fistula, what to eat and what to avoid, correct toilet habits, safe home remedies, and when you must see a doctor immediately.
content:
“I saw drops of blood after the toilet and got scared” — many people say this in a low voice at the clinic. Piles are so common that a large number of people get them at some point in life. Delaying treatment out of shame or hesitation is not right, because in the early stage diet and daily routine alone give a lot of relief.

It is also important to know that not every cause of bleeding from the anus is piles — so do get a proper check-up once. This article is for information only — take treatment only on the advice of your Vaidya or doctor.

What are piles?

There are clusters of veins (blood vessels) around the anus and rectum. When these veins swell up due to straining at stool, constipation or pressure, it is called piles (haemorrhoids). There are two main types:

  • Internal piles — inside the rectum; often bright red blood comes during stools without pain, and sometimes the pile comes out and goes back by itself or with a finger
  • External piles — outside the anus; itching, burning, swelling and pain while sitting; sometimes a blood clot forms in it, causing sudden severe pain and a hard lump

In a fissure (a small tear in the anus) there is sharp, cutting pain during and after stools, and in a fistula (bhagandar) pus or fluid comes out again and again from an opening near the anus. These three are different diseases with different treatments, so correct identification by examination is necessary.

The Ayurvedic view

In Ayurveda, piles are called Arsha. The meaning of the name itself tells us that this disease troubles a person like an enemy:

अरिवत् प्राणिनो मांसकीलका विशसन्ति यत् ।
अर्शांसि तस्मादुच्यन्ते गुदमार्गनिरोधतः ॥
— Ashtanga Hridaya, Nidana Sthana 7

Meaning: Because these fleshy pegs (piles) that obstruct the anal passage torment a person like an enemy (ari), they are called “Arsha”.

According to Ayurveda, the root cause of Arsha is weak Agni. Weak Agni leads to constipation and retention of stool, Apana Vayu gets disturbed, and the three doshas collect in the veins of the anus to form piles. Vata-type piles are dry, hard and painful; in Pitta-type there is more burning and bleeding (raktarsha); in Kapha-type the piles are soft, swollen and itchy. Acharya Sushruta described four ways of treating Arsha — medicine, kshara (alkaline preparation), agnikarma (thermal cautery) and surgery — and which one is suitable is decided only after seeing the stage.

Main causes

  • Chronic constipation and straining at stool; frequent diarrhoea too
  • Lack of fibre and water in food; maida, junk food, very spicy food
  • Sitting for long hours, sitting long in the toilet with a mobile
  • Pregnancy and childbirth; older age; obesity
  • Lifting heavy weights, long-standing cough or straining to pass urine
  • Alcohol, smoking, staying up late at night and lack of exercise

Symptoms and tests

  • Drops or a stream of bright red blood during or after stools
  • Itching, burning, heaviness or dampness at the anus
  • A wart-like swelling near the anus that comes out during stools
  • Pain while sitting or walking, sometimes sudden severe pain and a hard bluish lump

The doctor or Vaidya examines the anus (a finger examination, and if needed with a proctoscope) to identify piles, fissure or fistula. A haemoglobin test checks for anaemia, and a colonoscopy may be advised if bleeding occurs after 45–50 years, bowel habits change, or there is a family history of bowel cancer.

Diet: what to eat, what to avoid

The most important thing in piles is — keeping the stool soft and not letting constipation happen. According to Ayurveda, light, fibre-rich food that keeps Agni balanced is beneficial.

What to eat

  • Enough water through the day (in kidney or heart disease ask your doctor about the amount)
  • Atta with bran, dalia, jowar, bajra; pulses with husk
  • Green vegetables — bottle gourd, ridge gourd, spinach, pointed gourd, suran (elephant foot yam, well cooked)
  • Fruits — papaya, guava, pear, apple, fig; soaked raisins
  • Fresh thin buttermilk with lunch — Ayurveda specially praises buttermilk (takra) for Arsha
  • A little desi ghee in food (in heart disease or high cholesterol ask your doctor)

What to avoid

  • Very spicy, chilli-masala, oily-fried food — these can increase burning and bleeding
  • Maida, biscuits, pizza, noodles, too much non-vegetarian food
  • Alcohol, smoking and too much tea-coffee
  • Stale, heavy and late-night food

Correct toilet habits and daily routine

  • Go as soon as the urge comes, do not postpone it; and do not strain forcefully without an urge
  • Do not sit in the toilet for more than 5 minutes; do not take a mobile or newspaper along
  • Keep a small stool under your feet so that the knees stay above the hips
  • After stools, wash gently with lukewarm water; do not rub with rough toilet paper
  • Walk or exercise 30 minutes daily; do not sit continuously for very long, walk a little every hour
  • Keep weight under control; do not hold your breath while lifting heavy weights

Yoga

Pavanamuktasana, Malasana, Vajrasana (after meals), Bhujangasana, Anulom-Vilom and Ashwini mudra (gently contracting and relaxing the anal muscles) are considered helpful. Caution: during bleeding, in severe pain, in pregnancy or after a recent operation, do any pose only after asking your doctor; learn yoga from a trained teacher.

Safe home remedies

  • Sitz bath (kati snana): sitting in a tub of lukewarm water for 10–15 minutes, 2–3 times a day — gives relief in burning, itching and pain
  • Isabgol husk: with enough water, to keep stools soft — never take it without water, and keep a gap of about 2 hours from other medicines
  • Buttermilk and fibre-rich food: in the daily diet
  • Cleanliness: keep the anal area dry and clean; wear loose cotton clothes

Ask your Vaidya/doctor before applying any paste, oil or home item on the anus — many things can increase irritation. These remedies are only supportive; if there is no improvement in two weeks, get examined.

Ayurvedic treatment — with caution

Ayurveda mentions several medicines for Arsha, such as — Haritaki (harad), Triphala, preparations made with suran (elephant foot yam), Nagkesar, and classical formulations like Abhayarishta and Arshoghni vati. For large or repeatedly prolapsing piles and for fistula, Ayurvedic surgical procedures like Ksharasutra and Ksharakarma are done by a trained surgical specialist. However:

  • Which medicine or procedure, in what dose and for how long — the Vaidya/surgeon decides this only after looking at the type and stage of piles and the person's prakriti, pulse, age and current medicines.
  • Do not stop your current medicines on your own — especially blood thinners (such as aspirin); if there is bleeding, talk to your doctor about them.
  • Do not take strong laxatives day after day — frequent diarrhoea also worsens piles; avoid roadside or unqualified “burning/cutting of piles” treatments — they carry a risk of infection, heavy bleeding and narrowing of the anus.
  • In pregnancy, breastfeeding, children and the elderly, give any medicine only on the advice of a Vaidya/doctor. Beware of claims like “sure cure without operation” or “piles removed from the root”.

When to see a doctor immediately

  • Heavy bleeding during stools, dizziness or weakness — go to hospital immediately
  • Black, tar-like stools, or blood mixed in the stool (not just drops on the surface)
  • Bleeding for the first time after 45–50 years, a change in bowel habit, weight loss or a family history of bowel cancer
  • Sudden very severe pain and a hard bluish-black lump, or a prolapsed pile that does not go back
  • Painful swelling near the anus with fever, or discharge of pus (abscess/fistula)
  • Anaemia, or bleeding that continues even after two to three weeks of measures

Summary — points to remember

  • Do not let constipation happen — water, fibre, fruits-vegetables and buttermilk
  • Do not strain at stool; do not sit long in the toilet
  • Lukewarm water sitz bath; less spicy-fried food and alcohol
  • If there is bleeding, get examined at least once — not all bleeding is piles
  • Medicines and procedures like Ksharasutra only from a qualified Vaidya/surgeon
